claims.label: Algorithm 2 / Theorem 3.1 expected approximation guarantee
claims.gist: The displayed Algorithm 2 uses one shared candidate pool across its outer rounds and permanently removes selections assigned to discarded candidates.
claims.statement: Under the displayed Algorithm 2 and Theorem 3.1 parameter conditions, the expected returned value is at least \((1/e-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\).
conditions: \(\varepsilon=0.1\), \(\ell=10\), \(k=1000\), and \(m=\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor=100\) satisfy the theorem's displayed numerical conditions.
The objective is the nonnegative modular function \(f(S)=|S\cap H|\), with \(|H|=1000\) and at least 9000 zero-value elements including the 2000 dummies.
claims.quantifiers: The approximation guarantee is stated for instances satisfying Theorem 3.1; the modular instance below is legal and has \(\operatorname{OPT}=1000\).

result.summary: On a legal modular instance, the displayed Algorithm 2 returns value \(100\) in expectation, below the Theorem 3.1 requirement of \((1/e-0.1)\cdot1000\approx267.879\).
result.witness: Let \(H\) contain 1000 unit-value elements and provide at least 9000 zero-value elements including the 2000 dummies. Set \(f(S)=|S\cap H|\). Then \(\operatorname{OPT}=1000\). With \(\varepsilon=0.1\), \(\ell=10\), \(k=1000\), and \(m=100\), the first round performs \(m\ell=1000\) greedy selections from a single shared pool \(V\). These exhaust \(H\), assigning exactly 100 elements of \(H\) to each of the ten candidates. One candidate is retained at random, but the 900 high-value elements assigned to discarded candidates have already been removed from \(V\). All later marginal gains are zero. Therefore \(\mathbb{E}[f(\text{returned set})]=100\), while the claimed lower bound is \((1/e-0.1)\cdot1000\approx267.879\).
result.argument: Because all remaining high-value elements have marginal one while zero-value elements have marginal zero, the first round consumes all of \(H\). Retaining one candidate cannot recover high-value elements already deleted from the shared pool. The returned value is exactly \(100\) regardless of which candidate is retained, contradicting the displayed approximation guarantee.
not_claimed: Empirical results are not claimed invalid.
The defect is not generalized beyond the displayed Algorithm 2 / Theorem 3.1 connection.
The corrected arXiv version has not yet been independently checked because it had not been posted when this version of the record was released.
result.repair_note: The responding author states that the analysis assumes the candidate pool is restored at the start of each outer round, \(V\leftarrow U\setminus G\), as in Algorithms 7 and 10. The authors report that with this repair the proof goes through and Theorem 3.1 is unchanged.

claims.label: Algorithm 5 Update termination as called by Algorithm 6
claims.gist: Algorithm 6 calls Algorithm 5 Update on an empty residual candidate pool before testing whether its threshold has fallen below \(\tau_{\min}\).
claims.statement: Algorithm 5 Update terminates when called by Algorithm 6 under its stated inputs.
conditions: The objective is modular with one singleton of value \(M>0\) and all other elements, including dummies, of value zero.
\(\ell=2\), \(\varepsilon=0.1\), \(k\) is sufficiently large and legal, and \(\tau_{\min}=\varepsilon M/k>0\).
claims.quantifiers: This finding is a concrete nontermination trace for a legal execution under Theorem 4.1 inputs; it is separate from the Algorithm 2 approximation counterexample.

result.summary: After the singleton is selected and removed from every candidate pool, Algorithm 6 can call Update on an empty active residual pool before its cutoff test. Algorithm 5 has no cutoff inside its empty-candidate loop. With zero residual marginal gains, \(\tau_j^{(t)}=0.9^tM>0\) for every finite \(t\), so Update does not terminate and never returns to the cutoff test.
result.witness: Initially each \(V_j\) contains the positive singleton and \(\tau_j=M\). The first alternating-addition step selects that singleton and removes it from every candidate pool. At a later active empty residual pool, Algorithm 6 calls Update before checking \(\tau_j<\tau_{\min}\). Algorithm 5 then repeatedly reduces \(\tau_j\) by the factor \(1-\varepsilon=0.9\) while the residual candidate set remains empty. Since \(\tau_j=0.9^tM>0\) for every finite \(t\) and there is no cutoff within the loop, Update never terminates. This is a separate defect from the Algorithm 2 witness.
result.argument: The nontermination follows from the order of operations in Algorithm 6 and the absent cutoff in Algorithm 5 Update. The positive singleton is selected first; thereafter all residual marginal gains are zero. The Update loop therefore cannot satisfy its nonempty-candidate condition at any finite iteration and does not return to Algorithm 6's cutoff test.
not_claimed: Empirical results are not claimed invalid.
The defect is not generalized beyond the displayed Update / Algorithm 6 control flow, except that the authors state the same repair also covers PItG (Algorithm 11), which calls Algorithm 6.
The corrected arXiv version has not yet been independently checked because it had not been posted when this version of the record was released.
result.repair_note: The responding author states that Algorithm 5 is missing the \(\tau_{\min}\) cutoff and should stop once \(\tau<\tau_{\min}\). The authors report that this guard preserves the adaptivity and query bounds and also covers PItG (Algorithm 11), which calls Algorithm 6.
